prompt: Match each task to the shape of its answer.

pairs.right: a group number with no name
a ranked list of other things

right_distractors: a yes from a person who checked

prompt: A report stored each member's k-means group last month and compares it with this month's. What goes wrong?

choices.text: Group numbers are not stable across runs
choices.why: Right. Group 6 last month and group 6 this month can be different readers. Store the run beside the id.

choices.text: k-means refuses to run twice on the same members
choices.why: It runs as often as you like; the trouble is what its numbers mean.

choices.text: The silhouette falls every month, so the groups get worse
choices.why: Nothing says the silhouette falls; the problem is the ids, whatever the score.

choices.text: The report needs a label to compare clusters
choices.why: Clustering has no label at all; the ids are the problem.

prompt: Why is a recommendation keyed by a pair rather than by a member?

choices.text: Two members share every recommendation
choices.why: Each member gets their own list.

choices.text: Each member has one score per title they might be shown
choices.why: Right. Eighty titles means up to eighty scores a member.

choices.text: The pair is the member and the cutoff, the same as for lapsing
choices.why: The cutoff is there too, but the pair that makes it big is member and title.

choices.text: Recommendations are computed for pairs of titles, never for people
choices.why: Pairs of titles are counted, but the answer is a list for a person.

prompt: In classify.py, what does make_pipeline give you?

choices.text: A faster logistic regression
choices.why: The algorithm is unchanged; the pipeline joins the steps.

choices.text: A way to train on several cutoffs at once
choices.why: It trains on whatever rows fit is given, here one cutoff.

choices.text: One object that scales, encodes and predicts, fitted together
choices.why: Right. The scaling learned in September is the one applied in November.

choices.text: A scheduled job that retrains the model
choices.why: Nothing in it is scheduled; that is the platform's job in later lessons.

prompt: At the default threshold the model calls 248 members lapsed and 530 lapsed. Why does the platform store probabilities rather than classes?

choices.text: Classes take more disk than probabilities
choices.why: A 0 or 1 is smaller, if anything.

choices.text: predict_proba is the only one scikit-learn can save to a file
choices.why: Both are just numbers; the reason is the threshold.

choices.text: Probabilities are always right, and classes are guesses
choices.why: Both come from the same model; one has a threshold baked in.

choices.text: A stored class freezes the threshold into every row
choices.why: Right. With probabilities, the threshold is a parameter of whoever reads the table.

prompt: What threshold does scikit-learn's predict compare the probability with, for two classes?
A model reads support tickets and answers delivery, payment or refund. What changes compared with the lapse model?

choices.text: Three probabilities instead of two
choices.why: Right. It is multi-class classification, and nothing else changes.

choices.text: It becomes regression, because there are more than two answers
choices.why: Three categories are still categories.

choices.text: It needs clustering first to find the three classes
choices.why: The classes are known and labelled; nothing has to be found.

choices.text: predict_proba stops working with more than two classes
choices.why: It returns one probability per class.

prompt: Why not encode home_shop as Paulista 0, Pinheiros 1, Cambuí 2 and so on?

choices.text: scikit-learn raises an error on integer categories
choices.why: It does not; that is why the mistake is silent.

choices.text: The model would treat the shops as an order with distances
choices.why: Right. Cambuí would be twice Pinheiros, an order that does not exist.

choices.text: Seven numbers take more memory than seven columns
choices.why: It is the other way round, and memory is not the issue.

choices.text: SQLite cannot store a shop as a number
choices.why: It can; the problem is what the model reads into the number.

prompt: Into how many columns did encode.py turn channel, age_band and home_shop?
A model trained before September 2025 meets a member whose channel is app. What does handle_unknown="ignore" do?

choices.text: It retrains the encoder with the new value
choices.why: Nothing retrains at prediction time.

choices.text: It raises an error on the first app member
choices.why: That is what happens without it.

choices.text: It encodes the channel as all zeros
choices.why: Right. The model then knows nothing about the channel, and keeps answering.

choices.text: It treats app as store, the most common channel
choices.why: It maps the unknown value to no channel at all, not to the commonest.

prompt: Which of these are true of one-hot encoding in encode.py? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Each value of a category gets its own column
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Exactly one column of each group holds a 1
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The columns are learned from the rows it was fitted on
choices.why: Right. A later value has no column.

choices.text: Larger shops get larger numbers
choices.why: No column is bigger than another; that is the point.

prompt: Why does regress.py fill a missing spend_next_90d with 0?

choices.text: LinearRegression cannot read missing values, so any number would do
choices.why: The number matters: zero is chosen because it is true here.

choices.text: To remove those members from the training rows
choices.why: They stay, with a label of 0.

choices.text: Because the query only returns members who lapsed
choices.why: It returns members who spent something after the cutoff.

choices.text: A member with no visit in the 90 days spent nothing
choices.why: Right. In another dataset missing means unknown, and zero would teach something false.

prompt: What was regress.py's mean absolute error, in reais?
Members 2 and 3 had identical histories and spent R$ 39.90 and R$ 229.60 afterwards. What does that say about the model?

choices.text: Nothing it sees tells them apart
choices.why: Right. The error spreads around the truth; the useful question is how wide.

choices.text: That it is broken, since it predicted almost the same for both
choices.why: Identical inputs give near-identical outputs; that is correct behaviour.

choices.text: That it needs to be a classifier instead
choices.why: The answer is still an amount.

choices.text: That members 2 and 3 should be removed as outliers
choices.why: They are ordinary members; the future is just not in their history.

prompt: What is the baseline for a regression?

choices.text: The previous version of the model
choices.why: That is a comparison worth making too, but it is not the baseline.

choices.text: The training label's average, predicted for everybody
choices.why: Right. It uses no features at all.

choices.text: A regression with only the most important feature
choices.why: Any feature makes it more than the dumbest prediction.

choices.text: Zero, because spending nothing is the commonest outcome
choices.why: For regression the baseline is the mean; the commonest class is the classifier's baseline.

prompt: By how many reais per member did the regression beat everybody spends the average?
Why does the platform keep computing the baseline after the model ships?

choices.text: Because scikit-learn deletes the dummy models after training
choices.why: Nothing is deleted; the baseline moves with the data.

choices.text: The baseline replaces the model when the model fails
choices.why: It is a yardstick, not a fallback.

choices.text: The baseline moves, and a model looks better while knowing less
choices.why: Right. Lesson 9 tracks the model and the baseline on the same rows.

choices.text: Regulators ask for one in every report
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson is about regulation.

prompt: What does the silhouette score need that k-means does not have?

choices.text: A label for each member
choices.why: It needs no label, which is why it is used to compare values of k.

choices.text: A second run with a different seed
choices.why: One run is enough.

choices.text: The number of categories in the shop
choices.why: It knows nothing about categories, only distances.

choices.text: Nothing more than the rows and their groups
choices.why: Right. It compares each member's distance to its own group and to the next one.

prompt: At which k did the silhouette peak in cluster.py?
Every member has two favourite categories, yet the eight groups each centre on one. What does that show?

choices.text: The silhouette found what it could see, not everything there
choices.why: Right. The second favourite is spread at 7 or 8% across every group.

choices.text: That the generator gives each member only one favourite
choices.why: It gives two; the second is drawn for fewer books.

choices.text: That k = 28 would have given a silhouette of 1
choices.why: Nothing measured says so; the peak was at 8.

choices.text: That clustering on shares cannot work at all
choices.why: It found a real structure: the first favourite.

prompt: Why does recommend.py divide each co-purchase count by the recommended title's popularity?

choices.text: To keep the scores between 0 and 1
choices.why: They are not kept in any range; the point is what they compare.

choices.text: Otherwise everybody gets the same bestsellers
choices.why: Right. It asks whether B goes with A more than B sells anyway.

choices.text: Popular titles are out of stock more often
choices.why: The shop has no stock in it.

choices.text: To recommend only titles nobody has bought
choices.why: A title nobody bought has no count to divide.

prompt: What hit rate at 5 did the co-purchase recommender reach, in percent?
The co-purchase list hit 67.1% against 21.0% for popularity. Which conclusion does that NOT support?

choices.text: That it ranks members' next titles better than popularity
choices.why: That is exactly what hit rate measures.

choices.text: That the shop's members have regular taste
choices.why: The lesson says so, and it helps the number.

choices.text: That showing the list would cause those sales
choices.why: Right. Nobody was shown it; only an experiment says whether it changes anything.

choices.text: That the test used only purchases after 30 November
choices.why: That is how it was built: count before, judge after.

prompt: Put the steps of recommend.py's test in order.
items: split each member's titles at 30 November
count pairs of titles bought before the cut
recommend five titles each member did not own
check them against what they bought after

prompt: Match each task at Ponto Final to when its right answer is known.

pairs.right: never: there is no right answer
when the member next buys, if ever

right_distractors: the moment the model is trained

prompt: Which task needs features that are minutes old rather than a day old?

choices.text: The lapse model, because members leave suddenly
choices.why: Lapsing plays out over 90 days; a day-old feature is fine.

choices.text: Clustering, because group numbers change every run
choices.why: A month-old grouping is fine; unstable ids are a different problem.

choices.text: The spend regression, because money is involved
choices.why: It works on 90-day windows, like lapsing.

choices.text: The recommender
choices.why: Right. A purchase at 10:02 should change what the site shows at 10:05.

prompt: A lapse score table has member_id and p_lapse and nothing else. What can it never be used for?

choices.text: Comparing the scores with the outcomes 90 days later
choices.why: Right. Without the cutoff, nobody knows which 90 days to compare with.

choices.text: Sending vouchers to the top hundred
choices.why: Ranking needs only the scores.

choices.text: Choosing a threshold other than 0.5
choices.why: Probabilities are exactly what makes that possible.

choices.text: Joining the scores to the members table
choices.why: member_id joins it.

prompt: A lapse model reaches 82% on some measure. What is the first thing to ask?

choices.text: Which algorithm produced it
choices.why: The algorithm matters less than what the number is compared with.

choices.text: What the baseline scores on the same rows
choices.why: Right. Always stays already scores 83% on the most common measure.

choices.text: Whether it was trained on more than 3,000 members
choices.why: Size does not make a number meaningful.

choices.text: Whether 82% rounds up to 85%
choices.why: Rounding changes nothing about what it means.
